## What is compiled?

Native ROME calls compiled C through R's `.C` interface. Our coordinate
search, coefficient sweeps, scale block and support polishing are compiled
with Numba's `njit`, which requires compilation without Python object mode.
The Python path loop dispatches one compiled solve per penalty. Its first-use
compilation is excluded from the timings. The boundary LP is solved by SciPy's
compiled HiGHS backend. Thus the observed difference is not interpreted-code
execution versus C. Native ROME handles the entire path in one compiled call;
our current Python driver dispatches each penalty separately.
The Python, R and installed ROME shared-library binaries are all x86-64 in
this environment; a mixed-architecture comparison is not the explanation.

## Different amounts of work

The checked ROME source is commit
`99d6f07e2f5daa262768387701af7769dfbc2212`. Its
`ecd_huber_benchmarktest_` branch is selected by the Figure1 call:
`adapt=FALSE`, adaptive screening and KKT checks. It stops inner sweeps when
$$
\max_j\left\{\frac{\|x_j\|_2^2}{n}
(\beta_j^{k+1}-\beta_j^k)^2\right\}
<\epsilon\sum_i h_{0.5}(y_i).
$$
Its subsequent KKT repair checks predictors outside the included set. This
is different from our full current coefficient stationarity requirement at
$10^{-6}$. The numerical value `eps=1e-4` is not a KKT tolerance and cannot
be directly equated to the Python tolerance. In particular, the original
right-hand side depends on sample size and the unscaled null loss.

ROME retains its included predictors and screening information across
penalties and caches predictor squares and thresholds for the whole path.
Python currently initializes its working set to all predictors at each new
penalty, then drops zero coefficients within that solve and repairs the set
using full KKT checks. Transferring suitable screening and cached predictor
quantities across penalties is a concrete optimization opportunity, provided
screening is rechecked when scale changes.

For each visited coordinate, ROME's C primitive allocates and sorts all
$2n$ Huber knots. Python first tests a local affine root and verifies that
it remains in the current Huber cell. A verified root is an exact coordinate
solution and avoids sorting. Otherwise it invokes the exact knot sweep.
The current fallback allocates knot/jump arrays and sorts its forward knots;
there is also scope to reuse those buffers. Python additionally uses optional
support Newton polishing; both Python modes in Figure1 use the same setting.

## Measured examples

{{< include outputs/implementation-audit/timings.qmd >}}

These examples are individual datasets, not replication averages. Joint LP
share is directly measured CPU time inside boundary LP calls divided by total
prepared path CPU. It includes repeated boundary solves along the path.
Other differences, including iteration counts, screening, knot sorting and
polishing, are source-level mechanisms; this audit does not assign them
separate timing percentages without a component profiler.

{{< include outputs/implementation-audit/work.qmd >}}

Native sweep counts come from separate deterministic reruns with the same
settings, checked against the saved native coefficient paths. Python counts
come from the primary timing records. A sweep need not visit the same set
of coordinates in the two implementations. Counts explain work differences;
they are not equal-cost operations, and joint LP work is additional.

One specific optimization opportunity is avoiding repeated boundary LPs.
For a certified zero-scale solution with $X\beta=y$, decreasing the penalty
from $\lambda$ to $\lambda'$ permits scaling its feasible dual by
$\lambda'/\lambda$. The primal and dual objectives both scale by the same
factor, so the same coefficient vector remains optimal. More generally,
the rescaled dual supplies a checkable gap for a reused boundary candidate.
The audit records where this check would pass on saved solutions. It does
not change the timed solver or claim a measured speedup from that opportunity.

{{< include outputs/implementation-audit/reuse-findings.qmd >}}

## A verified coordinate-level discrepancy

The original C coordinate function is also checked independently. Consider
$x=(1,1,1)^\top$, partial residual $u=(-1,0.2,0.5)^\top$,
$\delta=0.5$ and penalty $0.1$. The coordinate objective is
$$
g(b)=\frac13\sum_{i=1}^3h_{0.5}(u_i-b)+0.1|b|.
$$
At zero, the smooth derivative is $-1/15$, which lies in $[-0.1,0.1]$;
therefore $b=0$ is a global minimizer. The pinned C primitive returns
$b=0.0823529411764706$, with objective excess approximately $0.005006$.
Our coordinate routine and independent scalar optimization return zero.
The source interpolates derivative values across knots without explicitly
handling the L1 subgradient jump at zero in this case.

The installed R package reproduces the nonzero result when screening is
disabled. With adaptive screening it returns zero on this single-variable
example, because the coordinate can be screened out. Thus this is a verified
primitive and unscreened-entry discrepancy, not a claim that every screened
ROME fit is affected. The audit checks 22 declared coordinate fixtures,
including a repeated-pattern zero-optimum example with $n=100$;
that sample is not a whole-package failure-rate estimate. Native ROME remains
unchanged throughout the timing experiment.

## Interpretation

Our fixed-scale Python solver is not uniformly slower. Where joint Python
is much slower, measured boundary LP work can dominate. Where fixed Python
is slower, different stopping accuracy and substantial coefficient work on
correlated data must be examined before attributing the difference to the
compiler. Current native-runtime comparisons therefore need their explicit
accuracy qualification. The source discrepancy is a further reason to check
objectives and stationarity independently, rather than copying native returns
as unquestioned reference solutions.

## Reproduction

After `make figure1-complete`, run `python analysis/implementation_audit.py`
and render this report. Raw coordinate checks, an installed-R reproduction,
selected path timings, source hashes and a compiled verbatim C test primitive
are retained under `analysis/outputs/implementation-audit/`.
